einzeiler: How a single 60-word sentence written after 9/11 became the legal basis for decades of…
kurzfassung: A single sentence containing sixty words, drafted immediately after the September 11 attacks, became the primary legal foundation for decades of American military action worldwide. Congress overwhelmingly approved the measure in 2001, with only one representative dissenting after agonizing over its broad and undefined scope. Over the years, executive branches stretched the text to justify detentions, drone strikes, and conflicts against groups never mentioned in the original legislation.
stichpunkte: A White House lawyer copied a 1991 Gulf War template into a Word document to draft the Authorization for Use of Military Force.
The resulting sixty-word sentence was rushed through Congress within seventy-two hours of the September 11 attacks.
Representative Barbara Lee cast the lone dissenting vote in Congress, warning that the language was dangerously open-ended.
Legal experts note that words like detention and associated forces never appeared in the original text but were later read into it.
Top secret video teleconference meetings involving numerous officials and lawyers determine individual targets using profiles nicknamed baseball cards.
Successive presidential administrations used the same authorization to expand military operations into countries like Yemen, Somalia, and Libya.
Despite calls from various politicians to repeal or revise the authorization, attempts to replace it have repeatedly stalled.
The original 2001 authorization remains fully active and legally intact decades after its initial passage.

clips.text: A White House lawyer searched for precedent on his computer and copied text from the 1991 Gulf War to create a draft template.
The final vote count in the House of Representatives resulted in an overwhelming majority in favor, with a single member dissenting.

clips.hook: Guantanamo Bay and the missing words
clips.text: Thousands of individuals faced prolonged detention without charges even though the underlying authorization never mentioned detention.
Classified target profiles containing photographs and biographical statistics were reviewed during secure video meetings.
Congress eventually passed legislation to revoke a separate military authorization tied to the invasion of Iraq.

beschreibung:
We’re coming up on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, and it had us thinking about an episode we produced in 2014. It’s the story of one sentence, written in the hours after September 11th, 2001, that has led to the longest war in U.S. history. We examine how just 60 words of legal language have blurred the line between war and peace.
In the hours after the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, a lawyer sat down in front of a computer and started writing a legal justification for taking action against those responsible. The language that he drafted and that President George W. Bush signed into law—called the Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF)—has at its heart one single sentence, 60 words long. Over the last decade, those 60 words have become the legal foundation for the "war on terror." In this collaboration with BuzzFeed, reporter Gregory Johnsen tells us the story of how this has come to be one of the most important, confusing, troubling sentences of the last two decades. We go into the meetings that took place in the chaotic days just after 9/11, speak with Congresswoman Barbara Lee and former Congressman Ron Dellums about the vote on the AUMF. We hear from former White House and State Department lawyers John Bellinger & Harold Koh. We learn how this legal language unleashed Guantanamo, Navy Seal raids and drone strikes. And we speak with journalist Daniel Klaidman, legal expert Benjamin Wittes and Virginia Senator Tim Kaine about how these words came to be interpreted, and what they mean for the future of war and peace.
